slides.title: Why we need a mask
slides.body:
Standard self-attention lets every token attend to every other token. For a decoder model that generates text one token at a time, this is a problem: at position `t`, the model would 'see' tokens `t+1, t+2, ...` — the answer it's supposed to predict.

The **causal mask** (or 'autoregressive mask') prevents this leak. The rule: token at position `i` can only attend to positions `j ≤ i`.

In matrix form, the attention scores `S = Q · K^T` are masked so that all upper-triangular entries (where `j > i`) are set to `-inf` before softmax:

```
    j=0  j=1  j=2  j=3
i=0  s    -∞   -∞   -∞
i=1  s    s    -∞   -∞
i=2  s    s    s    -∞
i=3  s    s    s    s
```

With `-inf` going through softmax, those positions get weight 0 — equivalent to ignoring them entirely.

slides.title: Why -inf, not 0?
slides.body:
A common confusion: why mask with `-inf` and not just zero out the entries?

Because masking happens **before** softmax. If you set masked entries to 0, the softmax would still produce nonzero weight for those positions (`exp(0) = 1`). You'd be giving 'nothing' tokens nonzero attention.

Using `-inf` makes `exp(-inf) = 0`, so after softmax those positions have exactly zero weight. The remaining (unmasked) entries normalize cleanly.

In implementations, people often use a 'large negative number' like `-1e9` or `-1e4` instead of `-inf` for numerical stability. The effect is the same — softmax pushes those entries to (effectively) zero.

question.question: Why is the causal mask applied *before* softmax with `-inf`, rather than after softmax with multiplication by 0?
options: Multiplication by 0 is slower than `-inf` masking
After softmax, masking with 0 would leave the weights unnormalized; pre-softmax `-inf` masking integrates cleanly with the softmax normalization
There's no real difference; both work fine
question.explanation: Softmax normalizes by dividing by the sum of exp(scores). If you mask post-softmax with 0, the unmasked weights still sum to 1 — you're not actually removing the masked positions' contribution to the normalization. Pre-softmax `-inf` makes those positions contribute 0 to the sum, so the unmasked positions normalize over only the valid neighbors.

slides.title: Why this enables efficient training
slides.body:
The clever thing about causal masking: it lets you train on all positions of a sequence in **a single forward pass**.

At each position `t`, the model is computing `P(token_{t+1} | tokens_{1..t})`. With causal masking, position `t`'s computation is unaffected by anything at position `t+1, t+2, ...`. So during training, you can:

1. Run the full sequence through the model in one forward pass.
2. The loss is the sum of `-log P(token_{t+1} | tokens_{1..t})` for every position `t`.
3. Gradients flow back. Done.

This is why GPT-style models train so efficiently: one forward pass produces N next-token predictions (one per position), and the causal mask guarantees each prediction is based only on its allowed context.

Without the causal mask, you'd need a separate forward pass per training position. That's an N× slowdown.

slides.title: Inference: KV-cache and the mask
slides.body:
At inference (generation) time, the model is already only seeing left context — there's nothing in the future yet. So why keep the mask?

Two reasons:

1. **Behavior consistency.** The model was trained with the mask; removing it at inference would give the model strange new attention patterns it never saw.

2. **KV-cache efficiency.** With causal attention, the K and V vectors for previous tokens never change as you append new ones. You compute K_i and V_i once, cache them, and reuse them for every subsequent token. (See [[kv-cache]] for more.)

In practice, the mask is implicit at inference: you're generating one token at a time, so position `t` only has access to positions `1..t-1` anyway. The mask is critical at *training time*, where the full sequence is processed in parallel.

question.question: Why does causal masking let GPT-style training process all N positions in a single forward pass?
options: Because each position's prediction only depends on earlier positions; the mask ensures parallel computation is equivalent to N sequential autoregressive predictions
Because the loss is computed only at the last position
question.explanation: Causal masking is what enables 'one forward pass, N next-token predictions.' Each position computes its own loss against its own next token, and the mask ensures position t's computation doesn't depend on anything at position t+1 onward. This is the single biggest efficiency win of decoder-only models over older RNN-style sequence models.

slides.title: What's next
slides.body:
Causal masking is the small architectural detail that makes autoregressive generation possible and efficient. Combined with [[multi-head-attention]] and the rest of the [[transformer-block]], you have a working decoder.

Next: [[cross-attention]] — the encoder-decoder bridge — and [[training-objectives]], where we look at exactly what loss the model is minimizing.

Key takeaways:
- Causal mask sets `S[i, j] = -inf` for `j > i` before softmax
- It enables training on all N positions in a single forward pass
- It also enables the KV-cache at inference time
